passage:
"Anjali, did you see Bruno's gate was open?" Joseph ran up the stairs, out of breath.
"Yes. When I came back from tuition."
"And you didn't shut it?"
"I didn't open it! Mrs. Dsouza's cousin did. I just walked past."
"Bruno ran out on the main road. The watchman caught him near the bus stop."
Anjali twisted the strap of her bag. "But that's not my fault. If I had opened it, then it would be."
"You saw it, though."
"Seeing isn't doing." She stared at her shoes. "Is he okay?"
"His leg is scraped. Mrs. Dsouza was crying."
Anjali was quiet for a moment. "I thought someone else would shut it."
"I think that too, sometimes," Joseph said. "Come on. Let's go and tell her we're sorry."

qa.q: Where did Bruno run after getting out?
qa.a: Bruno ran out on the main road, and the watchman caught him near the bus stop.

qa.q: Why does Anjali feel it isn't her fault even though she saw the open gate?
qa.a: To her, opening the gate would be a real wrong, but walking past feels like doing nothing, so the guilt seems smaller. Twisting her bag strap and staring at her shoes show part of her feels bad anyway.

qa.q: What could Anjali try the next time she notices something like an open gate?
qa.a: Shut it or tell an adult right away, and remember that walking past a problem can hurt someone as much as causing it.

qa.q: What is it like for Mrs. Dsouza when she finds out Bruno was hurt?
qa.a: She is upset enough to cry 😢; for her, Bruno's scraped leg hurts just the same whether someone opened the gate or only left it open.

grounding: It shows a child feeling blameless for leaving a gate open that she only saw, while the harm to the dog happened all the same.

passage:
My name is Madhuri, and I still think about Gurpreet's volcano. Last week Gurpreet brought a volcano model to class. He had worked on it for a whole week, with cotton smoke and red paint lava. He left it on the edge of the bench near the window. At lunch the wind blew the curtain against it, and I saw it wobble. I thought, someone will move it. I didn't touch it. I went to get my tiffin.
When I came back, the volcano was on the floor, cracked in half. Gurpreet's face went red. Everyone asked who broke it, and I said, "Not me," and that was true. I didn't push it.
But at night I kept seeing that curtain flapping. I only had to slide the model back a little.

qa.q: What made Gurpreet's volcano wobble?
qa.a: The wind blew the curtain against it while it sat on the edge of the bench near the window.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri feel it was fair to say "Not me"?
qa.a: Madhuri hadn't pushed the model, so not moving it felt like doing nothing wrong, as if the wind was to blame. Seeing the curtain again at night shows the guilt was there anyway.

qa.q: What small step could Madhuri take now?
qa.a: Madhuri could tell Gurpreet what happened, say sorry and offer to help fix the volcano; next time, sliding something back takes a second and prevents the damage.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel on learning that someone saw the model wobble and walked away?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and let down, because a week of his work broke when one small move could have saved it.

grounding: It shows a child who let a classmate's model fall feeling less guilty than if Madhuri had pushed it, though the harm was the same.

passage:
Class 5B note, Thursday
During recess it started to rain. Kashish was sitting under the shed and could see Sachin's library book lying open on the garden bench. She watched it for a while and did not bring it in. By the bell it was soaked and the pages had stuck together.
When I asked, Kashish said, "I didn't leave it there, Ma'am. I just didn't pick it up." She looked honestly puzzled that it could have anything to do with her.
I asked her one question: if she had carried the book out into the rain herself, how would she feel? She went quiet, then said, "Bad. But it's the same book, na?"
Next step: she and Sachin will dry the pages together and explain to the librarian tomorrow. I will keep an eye on how she handles it.

qa.q: Whose book got soaked in the rain?
qa.a: Sachin's library book got soaked while it was lying open on the garden bench.

qa.q: What does Kashish's puzzled look suggest she believed?
qa.a: It suggests she truly thought the ruined book wasn't really her doing, because she hadn't put it there; not acting felt innocent to her.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Kashish see it differently?
qa.a: The teacher asked her to imagine carrying the book into the rain herself, so she could notice the harm was the same, and then set up a way for her to help repair it.

qa.q: What is it like for Sachin to find the book stuck together?
qa.a: Sachin has to face the librarian over a ruined book, and may wonder why nobody sitting nearby brought it in.

grounding: It shows a child who let a book get ruined feeling less guilty than if she had caused it, seen through a teacher's note.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today was sports day. Last week Miss Pinto pinned the race list on the board, and I saw that Yusuf's name wasn't there. He runs faster than anyone in our class. I thought, someone will tell her. It's not my job. I didn't write the list.
This morning Yusuf came in his white shoes and read the list three times. Then he sat on the steps and watched the whole race with his chin on his knees.
If I had rubbed his name off, I would be a really bad person. But I didn't do anything, so it's not my fault. Right?
Then why does my tummy feel funny every time I think about those steps?
Reena

qa.q: What did Reena notice about the race list last week?
qa.a: That Yusuf's name wasn't there.

qa.q: How does Reena seem to feel about staying quiet, and what shows it?
qa.a: Reena seems uneasy and a little guilty, telling the diary it's not Reena's fault but admitting to a funny feeling in the tummy when remembering Yusuf on the steps.

qa.q: When could Reena have acted, and what could Reena do now?
qa.a: When the list first went up, Reena could have told Miss Pinto; now Reena could tell Miss Pinto what happened so it doesn't happen again.

qa.q: What was sports day like for Yusuf?
qa.a: He came ready in his white shoes and then found he couldn't race, so he probably felt confused, left out and sad watching from the steps.

grounding: A child who noticed a classmate left off a race list feels less guilty for saying nothing than for causing it, though the harm is the same.

passage: In the small town of Kottarakkara, the boys played cricket every evening beside Mariamma's shop. On Tuesday a big hit from Sibi cracked the shop's glass jar of sweets, and Sibi ran. Only Thomas saw it. When Mariamma came out shouting, she found Chinmay standing nearest, bat in hand. "You again!" Chinmay said it wasn't him. Nobody backed him up. His father had to pay for the jar, and Chinmay was kept home from cricket for a week. Thomas told himself, I didn't break it. I didn't lie. I only kept quiet, and that's different. But every evening he looked at the empty spot where Chinmay usually stood at slip, and he bowled badly.

qa.q: Who actually cracked the glass jar of sweets?
qa.a: A big hit from Sibi cracked the jar, and Sibi ran.

qa.q: Why does Thomas feel keeping quiet is different from what Sibi did?
qa.a: He didn't break the jar or tell a lie, so doing nothing feels less guilty to him than causing the harm, even though Chinmay was punished either way.

qa.q: What choice could Thomas still make to put things right?
qa.a: He could tell Mariamma, or an adult he trusts, who really hit the ball, so Chinmay is cleared even if it comes late.

qa.q: What might the week at home have been like for Chinmay?
qa.a: He would likely feel it was unfair and lonely, punished for something he didn't do while nobody stood up for him.

grounding: A boy who saw who broke a jar stays silent while a friend is blamed, telling himself that not speaking is less wrong than doing the harm.
